sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Magic was a cosmological concept for the Celts. It is classically defined as actions or words done or spoken to bring about a change, usually in the external world. Magic was typically an individual pursuit. When a group performed a ritual, that was usually called religion. With the Celtic druids the boundary grew slippery, because one person might act for the good of all. A satire might drive an ungenerous king from his throne. The act looked like private vengeance, but it served the bard's duty to keep wealth flowing through the king. Individual Celts practiced two kinds of magic. Propitiatory magic kept bad events away. Intercessory magic drew good things near. People wore amulets from earliest times to ward off evil, and such amulets appear at La Tène and Hallstatt sites. Verbal magic took the form of curses. Some practices survive as superstitions in the present. Nicknames once kept loved ones hidden from Otherworld eyes, and thus safe from fairy kidnapping. People still leave rags, called clooties, at sacred wells or trees. Celtic deities often had magical powers. The Welsh magician-bard Gwydion turned flowers into a bride. The great magician Merlin could change his shape. In Ireland the sea god Manannán mac Lir could also change his shape.

okr.objective: Document magic as a cosmological concept and practice among the Celts.
